headline: Rescued Fishing Cat Returns to Wild in Bangladesh Conservation Milestone
meta_description: A severely injured fishing cat rehabilitated in Bangladesh has been released into the wild with a tracking collar, offering a potential blueprint for regional…
summary_short: After months of intensive care, a badly injured fishing cat rescued in Bangladesh was successfully released into the wild—offering a new model for protecting endangered…
body:
A male fishing cat that arrived at a Bangladesh rehabilitation center barely clinging to life has been returned to the wild, marking a rare success story for a species that faces mounting pressure across South Asia. The cat, rescued by the Bangladesh Forest Department in February 2026, was so severely injured and malnourished that staff at the Jankichara Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation Centre had little hope he would survive. His jaw was dislocated from being beaten by people, leaving him unable to feed himself and weighing just 11 pounds. After weeks of assisted tube feeding and veterinary care, the cat's condition transformed: he gained weight, recovered strength, and was eventually fitted with a satellite-tracking collar before being released into a tea estate bordering a freshwater wetland.

Fishing cats (Prionailurus viverrinus) are among the most threatened small wildcats in the world. Though roughly 7,500 may exist in the wild across India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, and neighboring countries, about 95% of their range falls outside protected areas. A troubling finding from recent research shows that nearly a third of all media reports about fishing cats between 2005 and 2021 documented their deaths, with almost half of those caused by "kill-on-sight" reactions from fish and duck farmers protecting their livelihoods.

What makes this rescue significant is how it was handled. Rather than releasing the cat immediately, conservationists kept it in a soft-release enclosure for over eight weeks to ensure a smooth transition. This careful protocol—paired with ongoing satellite monitoring—contrasts sharply with typical rescue practices, where rehabilitated animals often die in captivity or disappear into the wild with no follow-up. The Creative Conservation Alliance, which runs the center, sees this case as a potential template. With 135 tea estates spread across northeastern Bangladesh, the partnership model could transform densely populated regions into practical refuges for this endangered species.
quick_facts: Male fishing cat rescued in February 2026, weighed only 11 pounds at intake
Rehabilitated at Jankichara Wildlife Rescue Centre in northeastern Bangladesh
Released with satellite collar into tea estate bordering freshwater wetland
Roughly 95% of fishing cat range exists outside protected areas
Over 135 tea estates in northeastern Bangladesh could serve as conservation sites
